steps.title: Two systems, one argument
steps.html:
Everything in this stage has already been taught. Lesson 5 gave you the obligation system — must, have to, mustn’t, don’t have to, can, should. Lesson 6 gave you the deduction system — must have, can’t have, might have. In an argument both are working at once, and the difference between a strong speaker and a weak one is usually which system they reach for.

Arguing about a rule needs the obligation system, and it needs one extra step: should have to. People should pay more is advice to drivers. People should have to pay more is an argument about what the law ought to require. Only the second one is a position on the policy.

steps.title: Three moves worth stealing
steps.html:
• Concede, then object. You may well be right about the cost, but the same service should still cost the same. The concession costs nothing and makes the objection much harder to dismiss.
  • Remove the obligation your opponent assumed. Nobody has to buy a new car to benefit — hybrids get a fifth off. Half of all disagreements are about a duty that does not exist.
  • Reject the claim, not the person. That can’t be the whole story attacks the argument. You can’t be serious attacks the speaker, and nobody has ever changed their mind after hearing it.

steps.title: Напиши свой текст
steps.sub: Напиши ответ, затем сверься с образцом
steps.modelHtml:
Sir,

I am writing to support the council’s proposal to link parking charges to vehicle emissions, and to answer the objection raised in your pages last week.

That objection may well be right about who pays. The oldest cars do tend to belong to the people with the least money, and a charge that falls hardest on them would be difficult to defend. But it is not the charge the council has proposed. Nobody has to buy a new car to benefit: hybrids pay a fifth less from the first day, and residents on the lowest incomes are exempt altogether.

The stronger argument is the one nobody has made. A charge of this kind is an incentive rather than a punishment, and it is the only measure available to us that requires no new public spending at a time when the legislature is cutting it everywhere else.

If the scheme goes ahead, the revenue should have to be spent on buses and on nothing else. I would urge readers to say so before the vote on the fourteenth.

Yours faithfully,
